podcast.body: Written by Norman Whitfield, this song reached number three on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1971. Scholar and former disco DJ Alice Eccles credits "Smiling Faces Sometimes" as the first Black Power song to become a pop hit, indicating its crossover appeal to white audiences who purchased the record and played it on the radio. While ostensibly a song about general betrayal, its meaning depends on perspective; many African Americans interpreted it as a commentary on white people, particularly white liberals, cautioning against false friendships and hidden malice. "Don't let the handshake and the smile fool you take my advice. I'm only trying to school you."
